question: Can full-parameter Evolution Strategies match GRPO on small-LLM reasoning at comparable cost while preserving prior capabilities, and do update norm and threshold sparsity explain any retention difference?

key_findings.claim: Across the eight model-task cells, GRPO has the higher peak validation accuracy in seven; ES wins only Llama-3.2-1B GSM8K.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports ES/GRPO for Qwen-2.5-1.5B as 53.0/56.4 Countdown, 77.4/80.4 GSM8K, 59.1/63.2 MATH, and 15.2/18.2 OlympiadBench; for Llama-3.2-1B it reports 15.2/37.6, 55.2/53.8, 32.2/35.6, and 5.6/5.9.

anchors.section: Table 1 and Section 3.1, ES vs GRPO Comparison

key_findings.claim: The prose claim that ES is within 3–4 percentage points of GRPO for both models is contradicted by the paper's own Llama Countdown cell.
key_findings.evidence: Llama-3.2-1B Countdown is 15.2% for ES versus 37.6% for GRPO, a 22.4-point deficit. This is not a marginal exception: it is the largest gap in Table 1 and makes the blanket comparability statement false.

key_findings.claim: In the sole retention experiment, ES raises Countdown accuracy but HellaSwag accuracy falls after the new-task curve has largely plateaued, whereas the GRPO trajectory remains near 60–61% HellaSwag.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen-2.5-1.5B trained on Countdown, Figures 1–2 show ES HellaSwag moving from roughly 58–61% early to about 50% at iteration 500; Countdown is near its maximum by about iteration 200. GRPO checkpoints cluster at high Countdown and stable HellaSwag. The plotted decline is about 10 percentage points, not 10% relative to the best score.

key_findings.claim: Calling this a general or catastrophic continual-learning failure is substantially broader than the evidence.
key_findings.evidence: The paper evaluates one Qwen-2.5-1.5B run family, one acquisition task (Countdown), and one retention benchmark (HellaSwag), within a single fine-tuning run rather than a sequence of acquired tasks. No retention seed distribution, confidence interval, significance test, or second prior-capability benchmark is reported; the authors acknowledge the single-retention-task limitation.

key_findings.claim: ES checkpoints are about three orders of magnitude farther from the base checkpoint in Frobenius norm than the matched-iteration GRPO checkpoints.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 and the log-scale Figure A2 place ES near 10^2 and GRPO near 10^-1 by iteration 500, while both curves rise with iteration. The authors correctly describe this as an association between parameter displacement and HellaSwag decline.

key_findings.claim: The norm comparison does not causally explain forgetting because the algorithms are not matched for anchoring, effective update scale, or objective.
key_findings.evidence: GRPO includes an explicit reference-policy KL coefficient of 0.001, while the ES recipe has no corresponding base-weight or policy anchor and uses fixed sigma=0.001 and alpha=0.0005. Large absolute displacement is therefore partly built into the compared recipes; there is no norm-matched ES, KL-free GRPO, learning-rate sweep, or intervention that equalizes displacement and tests retention.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1.2–A.2.1, GRPO objective and setup

key_findings.claim: The reported ES-versus-GRPO update-density contrast is measured by a fixed absolute threshold, not structural zeros.
key_findings.evidence: For each tensor the paper calls an update sparse when |ΔW|<10^-6 and plots the percentage below that threshold. GRPO is described as near 95% sparse across groups while most ES components are far lower; LayerNorm is the main high-sparsity ES exception.

key_findings.claim: Norm and 'sparsity' are not independent explanations under this metric.
key_findings.evidence: Because ES updates are roughly 1000 times larger in norm, applying the same 10^-6 absolute threshold mechanically places more ES coordinates above threshold even if the normalized update shapes were identical. The paper does not normalize by tensor scale or update norm, sweep the threshold, compare quantiles, or test top-k support, so density may largely restate the scale result.

key_findings.claim: Equal population size and rollout count do not establish comparable compute.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix equates 30 ES population members with 30 GRPO rollouts because each supplies stochastic samples, but ES evaluates perturbed parameter populations and GRPO samples outputs then backpropagates token-level policy updates. The paper reports no FLOPs, generated tokens, wall time, GPU-hours, throughput, or peak memory for either method and uses premature stopping for GRPO.

key_findings.claim: The accuracy comparison lacks enough selection and uncertainty detail for a reliable algorithm ranking.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 uses peak validation accuracy and says 'previously found optimal hyperparameters' without reporting the search spaces, selection data, number of runs, seeds, dispersion, or test-set confirmation. Appendix A.2 says GRPO was configured for 500 epochs but stopped when validation appeared to plateau; Figure A3 is labeled mean accuracy yet supplies no run count or error band.

key_findings.claim: The written ES update is under-specified relative to its own description.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.1 first says the implementation uses ranked weight updates, then defines Z_n by reward z-scores and updates θ with α(1/N)ΣZ_nε_n. The displayed estimator has no explicit 1/σ factor and does not say that it is absorbed into α. This may be an implementation convention, but the paper does not reconcile the two weightings or the scale convention.

key_findings.claim: The KL appendix is a useful negative result: policy KL is not a cross-algorithm surrogate for forgetting in these runs.
key_findings.evidence: Within ES, KL from the base rises as HellaSwag falls, but GRPO shows stable prior-task accuracy across a broad and non-monotone KL range. The authors therefore conclude that KL is less reliable when comparing ES and GRPO, despite its within-ES association.

anchors.section: Appendix A.4.1, Catastrophic Forgetting and KL

key_findings.claim: The paper's strongest defensible result is a diagnostic case study, not a demonstrated universal ES failure mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: It establishes a clear co-occurrence in one setting among continued full-parameter ES training, growing displacement, more coordinates above a fixed threshold, and declining HellaSwag. It neither isolates update scale/density causally nor shows irreversible loss across tasks, models, ES variants, population sizes, regularizers, or matched policy divergence.

method.core_idea: Replicate recent full-parameter, seed-replayed ES fine-tuning and compare it with VERL GRPO on four rule-verifiable reasoning tasks, then follow a new-task/old-task curve and inspect checkpoint displacement and thresholded update density.
method.mechanism: ES samples 30 Gaussian full-parameter perturbations (sigma 0.001), evaluates deterministic responses with binary/format rewards, standardizes population rewards, restores the base weights, and accumulates a noise-weighted update with alpha 0.0005. GRPO uses 30 rollouts, relative group advantages, clipping, and reference-policy KL coefficient 0.001. Both train on 200 examples per task. Forgetting is operationalized as HellaSwag accuracy while Qwen-2.5-1.5B learns Countdown; ΔW is summarized by Frobenius norm and the fraction of entries below 10^-6.
assumptions: Thirty ES perturbations and thirty GRPO rollouts provide a fair compute and estimator-quality match.
Peak validation accuracy after separate prior hyperparameter selection is a fair method comparison.
HellaSwag alone is an adequate proxy for preservation of broad prior capabilities.
A single-task run in which prior accuracy declines is representative of catastrophic forgetting in continual deployment.
Absolute checkpoint Frobenius distance is comparable across optimizers and causally relevant to retention.
The percentage of coordinates below a common 10^-6 threshold measures update support independently of update scale.
GRPO's explicit KL anchor and ES's absence of an analogous constraint do not confound the optimizer comparison.
Early stopping, numerical precision, reward implementation, and validation selection affect both methods comparably.

techniques.role: Gradient-free forward-only fine-tuning through seed-replayed Gaussian perturbations and reward-weighted population updates.
Gradient-based reference comparator with 30 rollouts, clipped relative advantages, and KL regularization.
Binary answer extraction plus Countdown format/answer rewards for GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, and Countdown.
Plots HellaSwag and Countdown accuracy at checkpoints throughout one fine-tuning run.
Measures absolute parameter displacement from the base model across update count.
Counts entries with absolute ΔW below 10^-6 by layer and parameter group.
Relates base/fine-tuned policy KL on old and new tasks to checkpoint accuracy.

evaluations.setting: Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct trained on 200 examples for four reasoning tasks
evaluations.result: ES scores 53.0 Countdown, 77.4 GSM8K, 59.1 MATH, and 15.2 OlympiadBench.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO scores 56.4, 80.4, 63.2, and 18.2, winning all four by 3.0–4.1 points.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the same four-task protocol
evaluations.result: ES scores 15.2 Countdown, 55.2 GSM8K, 32.2 MATH, and 5.6 OlympiadBench.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO scores 37.6, 53.8, 35.6, and 5.9; ES wins GSM8K by 1.4 but loses Countdown by 22.4, contradicting the claimed universal 3–4-point proximity.

evaluations.setting: Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Countdown acquisition with HellaSwag retention over 500 iterations
evaluations.metric: New-task and prior-task accuracy at checkpoints
evaluations.result: ES reaches near-peak Countdown around iteration 200 while HellaSwag subsequently declines to about 50% by iteration 500.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO maintains approximately 60–61% HellaSwag while reaching high Countdown; no repeated-seed uncertainty or matched final new-task checkpoint is supplied.

evaluations.result: ES rises monotonically to roughly 9×10^1 by iteration 500.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO is roughly 9×10^-2 at iteration 500, about three orders smaller, but GRPO alone has explicit reference KL regularization.

evaluations.metric: Percentage of |ΔW|<10^-6 by Q/K/V/O, MLP, LayerNorm, and layer index
evaluations.result: Most ES groups have many more entries above threshold; LayerNorm is the high-sparsity exception.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO curves are described as near 95% below threshold, but the common absolute threshold is confounded by the 1000-fold norm difference.

evaluations.setting: Checkpoint policy-divergence appendix on Countdown and HellaSwag
evaluations.result: ES shows increasing KL and falling HellaSwag; its new-task accuracy rises then plateaus.
evaluations.baseline: GRPO prior accuracy stays stable over a broader, non-monotone KL range, a negative result against KL as a universal forgetting indicator.

evaluations.metric: Population/rollout count, nominal update count, and reported hardware
evaluations.result: Both use 30 stochastic samples; GRPO uses A6000/FSDP, batch 200, minibatch 32, and is stopped when validation appears to plateau.
evaluations.baseline: No wall-clock, generated-token, FLOP, GPU-hour, memory, or energy measurement establishes comparable compute.

limitations: Author-admitted: ES stochasticity is high at population size 30; larger populations may reduce variance and change the reported curves.
Author-admitted: forgetting is evaluated with only HellaSwag during Countdown training and does not capture multifaceted prior-capability loss.
Reviewer-inferred: the retention result uses one small model family/size, one acquisition task, and one old-task benchmark rather than sequential learning.
Reviewer-inferred: no seed counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or raw run trajectories accompany Table 1, Figures 1–4, or Figure A3.
Reviewer-inferred: 'peak validation accuracy' and visually judged premature stopping use evaluation data for selection; no held-out test-set result is identified.
Reviewer-inferred: the prior hyperparameter search, ranges, number of trials, and selection rule are absent, so relative tuning effort is unknown.
Reviewer-inferred: matching population size to rollout count does not match compute, generated tokens, estimator variance, or optimizer work.
Reviewer-inferred: GRPO has explicit policy KL regularization while ES has no analogous anchor, confounding optimizer identity with regularization.
Reviewer-inferred: a fixed 10^-6 threshold makes 'sparsity' dependent on update scale; no threshold sweep or scale-normalized support metric is reported.
Reviewer-inferred: the norm/density analyses are observational; no intervention shows that reducing either one restores retention.
Reviewer-inferred: the written ES estimator does not reconcile ranked versus z-score weights or state whether 1/sigma is absorbed into alpha.
Reviewer-inferred: GRPO and ES use different training machinery and potentially numerical precision, yet precision and optimizer-state details are incomplete.
Reviewer-inferred: the claim of approximately 10% HellaSwag loss appears to mean about 10 percentage points; relative loss from roughly 61% to 50% is closer to 18%.
Reviewer-inferred negative result: GRPO wins seven of eight task/model cells and the Llama Countdown gap is 22.4 points.
Reviewer-inferred negative result: the KL-forgetting relationship does not transfer from ES to GRPO in the appendix.
failure_modes: Unconstrained full-parameter perturbations can random-walk along weakly rewarded directions after the target reward has plateaued.
Continuing ES past the useful target-task window can trade retention for negligible new-task gain.
Binary rule rewards constrain only a narrow output property, leaving large parameter directions effectively unpenalized.
Small ES populations can yield high-variance global updates and unstable task or retention conclusions.
A fixed absolute density threshold can misdiagnose large-but-shape-similar updates as intrinsically less sparse.
Peak-validation reporting can favor noisy trajectories and hide final-checkpoint regressions.
GRPO's explicit KL anchor can make an unregularized ES comparison look like an inherent optimizer effect.
One old-task score can fall from interference, formatting drift, or calibration changes without demonstrating irreversible knowledge loss.
The displayed ES estimator can be misimplemented if the omitted perturbation-scale convention or reward weighting is interpreted literally.
Stopping criteria based on visible validation plateaus can produce unequal optimization horizons and selection bias.
Dense full-weight ES may fail even when low-rank, anchored, or subspace ES variants would retain capabilities.
reusable_insights: Plot acquisition and retention jointly across every checkpoint; a target-task plateau can reveal avoidable post-convergence drift.
Compare optimizers at matched target performance, matched policy KL, matched parameter displacement, and matched compute rather than update count alone.
Add an explicit initial-weight or policy anchor to gradient-free post-training and ablate its strength.
Treat fixed-threshold coordinate density as scale-dependent; report normalized quantiles, support at multiple thresholds, and tensor-relative thresholds.
Separate association from mechanism by intervening on norm, perturbation rank, population size, and update support while measuring retention.
Report final as well as peak accuracy and reserve a test set distinct from checkpoint/hyperparameter selection.
Use a retention panel spanning knowledge, instruction following, safety, calibration, and reasoning, plus sequential task acquisition.
Preserve negative cells such as Llama Countdown and the non-universal KL relationship rather than compressing them into average comparability claims.
Account for rollouts, tokens, forward/backward FLOPs, wall time, memory, and hardware when comparing forward-only and gradient-based algorithms.
Specify the exact ES estimator, including antithetic sampling, rank or z-score shaping, sigma normalization, precision, and seed handling.
open_questions: Does the HellaSwag drop recover later, making the behavior transient performance drift rather than irreversible forgetting?
How do population size, antithetic sampling, reward shaping, and perturbation rank change retention at matched target accuracy?
Can anchored weight decay, policy KL, replay, or elastic penalties prevent drift without sacrificing ES's memory advantage?
Does ES still forget more than GRPO when both are matched for final policy KL or Frobenius displacement?
Is fixed-threshold density predictive after normalizing each tensor by its update norm or weight scale?
Do the results replicate across larger models, instruction-tuning states, multiple acquisition tasks, and a broad retention suite?
How many runs generated each reported mean, and what is the between-seed distribution of peak and final performance?
What exact hyperparameter search and stopping rule was applied to each algorithm?
What are wall-clock time, total generated tokens, FLOPs, peak memory, and GPU-hours at matched accuracy?
Does sequential multi-task ES exhibit interference distinct from the within-run overtraining shown here?
Would a norm-matched ES update remain dense and still degrade retention?
Which parts of the ES appendix estimator are implementation conventions versus omissions in the displayed equations?

competitive_landscape.title: Overcoming Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning with Evolution Strategies
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest current follow-up directly re-evaluating this paper's ES-forgetting conclusion
competitive_landscape.difference: Schweighofer et al. report that prior-task performance often recovers, characterize the effect as drift rather than irreversible forgetting, find it can also occur under RL, and introduce Anchored Weight Decay to stabilize retention. It directly narrows the target paper's title-level claim and supplies the most important post-publication contradiction/mitigation.

competitive_landscape.title: Evolution Strategies at Scale: LLM Fine-Tuning Beyond Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct method predecessor whose full-parameter ES implementation and Countdown comparison are replicated
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. establish billion-parameter full-weight ES and report advantages over RL in sample efficiency, long-horizon rewards, reward hacking, and stability. The target paper adds multi-benchmark GRPO replication and retention diagnostics, but its relative ranking differs and it does not match the current predecessor's broader v3 evaluations.

competitive_landscape.title: Evolution Strategies at the Hyperscale
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct scalable-ES competitor using structured perturbations for billion-parameter models
competitive_landscape.difference: EGGROLL uses rank-r perturbations, proves high-dimensional consistency properties, and reaches near-inference throughput while remaining competitive with GRPO. The target studies dense full-parameter perturbations; therefore its density and forgetting diagnosis need not transfer to low-rank population members.

competitive_landscape.title: ESSA: Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct gradient-free LLM-alignment competitor that restricts the ES search subspace
competitive_landscape.difference: ESSA evolves only singular values of LoRA adapters and supports INT4/INT8 inference, reporting task and scaling gains over GRPO up to 32B. The target evolves all weights at 1–1.5B and studies retention, so it contributes a distinct failure audit but not a verdict on parameter-efficient ES.

competitive_landscape.title: RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest prior analysis of why on-policy RL retains old capabilities during new-task fine-tuning
competitive_landscape.difference: Shenfeld et al. compare RL with SFT across language and robotic models and argue that on-policy RL selects KL-minimal solutions, with theory and broader retention evidence. The target contrasts GRPO with ES and adds weight-space density/norm plots, but its explicit-KL GRPO versus unanchored ES design does not isolate the claimed optimizer mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct antecedent for the GRPO update-sparsity diagnostic used as the target paper's mechanism comparator
competitive_landscape.difference: Mukherjee et al. test seven RL algorithms and ten LLMs, find only 5–30% of parameters change materially, and validate that tuning the identified subnetwork recovers performance. The target transfers one fixed-threshold diagnostic to ES versus GRPO but does not perform the causal subnetwork or threshold-robustness tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational inference-memory gradient-free LLM fine-tuning competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: MeZO uses two in-place zeroth-order forward passes, scales experiments to 66B, and evaluates classification, multiple choice, and generation with full and parameter-efficient tuning. It establishes the broader memory-efficiency premise but does not study online reward optimization or forgetting; the target's ES-specific retention audit is complementary and much smaller-scale.
competitive_landscape.source_version: v3, revised 2024-01-11; first submitted 2023-05-27; NeurIPS 2023 oral

competitive_landscape.title: Derivative-Free Optimization for Low-Rank Adaptation in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct derivative-free low-rank LLM adaptation antecedent
competitive_landscape.difference: Jin et al. alternate derivative-free optimization over inserted low-rank attention modules and report memory/convergence benefits in few-shot tasks. It constrains the search dimension rather than perturbing every weight, so the target's global-drift result does not establish its retention behavior.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Editing at Scale Leads to Gradual and Catastrophic Forgetting
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct large-model sequential-weight-editing antecedent for the forgetting framing
competitive_landscape.difference: Gupta et al. study many sequential ROME/MEMIT factual edits and observe gradual then abrupt loss of prior edits and downstream abilities. The target shares authors and transfers the forgetting lens to ES, but its evidence is continued optimization on one task rather than sequential edits and does not demonstrate the same two-phase phenomenon.
competitive_landscape.source_version: v4, revised 2024-06-10; first submitted 2024-01-15; ACL 2024 Findings

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first comprehensive multi-task comparison of modern full-parameter ES with GRPO that explicitly measures forgetting curves, and claim that ES's much larger, denser updates explain catastrophic loss of prior abilities.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper adds four-task/two-model peak-accuracy tables, a Countdown–HellaSwag checkpoint trajectory, parameter Frobenius norms, layerwise threshold density, and KL plots to the Qiu et al. ES implementation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a focused warning and diagnostic case study: continued unanchored full-weight ES on Countdown coincides with HellaSwag decline and far larger parameter displacement than KL-regularized GRPO. Multi-task coverage is broader than the direct ES predecessor, but the forgetting experiment itself remains one model/task/retention metric, density is scale-confounded, and no causal mechanism is established. The direct May 2026 follow-up arXiv:2605.30148v1 is a major current threat: it reports recovery, non-ES-specific drift, and effective anchored mitigation, so 'ES leads to catastrophic forgetting' should be narrowed to an observed transient or unresolved drift risk under this exact recipe.

reviewer_notes: Read all 11 pages of the local PDF, including references, Appendix A.1–A.4, equations, reward definitions, hyperparameters, and supplementary Figures A1–A3; directly inspected result/figure pages 3–5 and 10–11. Official arXiv lists only v1 (submitted 2026-01-28), and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.20861v1 byte-matches the reviewed local PDF exactly at SHA-256 a55685a0b3d7cd51e4b2f20ffd83c9132139231efae2be62b39805da7cadde05. All 11 indexed pages have usable extracted text. Negative/contradiction audit preserves GRPO's seven-of-eight wins, the 22.4-point Llama Countdown gap, the 10-percentage-point versus 10%-relative wording, the non-universal KL result, absence of uncertainty/compute accounting, and the ranked-versus-z-score estimator ambiguity. Nine exact-version primary competitors were checked on official arXiv through 2026-08-23, including the later direct counter-analysis arXiv:2605.30148v1. The paper's GitHub code and Hugging Face collection resolved with HTTP 200 when checked, but their contents were not used to override what the reviewed PDF reports.
